items.name: Treadmill
items.description: A motorised running belt with adjustable speed and usually incline, for walking, jogging and running indoors.
items.adjustability: Speed and incline by console; some folding.
items.buying_tips: Look for a deck of at least 140 x 50 cm for running, a continuous-duty motor of 2.5 HP or more, and a good cushioned deck.
items.safety: Clip on the emergency stop key and straddle the belt when starting.

items.name: Walking pad
items.description: A slim, low, often folding treadmill without handrails, mostly for walking at a desk or in small spaces.
items.weight_options: Top speed 6–12 km/h; usually no incline
items.adjustability: Speed by remote or app; folds or slides under a sofa.
items.buying_tips: Check top speed and belt width; most are not built for running even if they claim a running mode.
items.safety: Keep the speed low enough to walk without holding on, as there are usually no rails.

items.name: Incline trainer
items.description: A treadmill built for steep uphill walking, often up to 30–40% incline and some with decline, for hiking-style cardio.
items.weight_options: Incline up to 30–40%; decline to −6% on some
items.adjustability: Speed and steep incline by console.
items.buying_tips: Worth it if you mostly walk; check the incline motor speed and that the deck stays stable at maximum incline.
items.safety: Don't hold the rails at steep inclines; slow down instead.

items.name: Curved / manual treadmill
items.description: A self-powered treadmill with a curved slat belt; you set the speed by where you run on the curve, ideal for sprints.
items.weight_options: Speed self-set; some add belt resistance levels
items.adjustability: Some have a resistance brake for sled-style pushes.
items.buying_tips: Commercial-grade units are heavy and expensive; try one first as the running feel takes getting used to.
items.safety: Step off to the side rails to stop; the belt keeps moving briefly.

items.name: Flat manual treadmill
items.description: A cheap, flat, self-propelled treadmill with a fixed slight incline; you push the belt with your legs, mainly for walking.
items.weight_options: Fixed incline ~5–10°; magnetic tension on some
items.adjustability: Tension knob on some models; folds.
items.buying_tips: Fine for walking without power; most are too short and jerky for running.
items.safety: The belt can feel stiff then lurch; hold the rails when starting.

items.name: Anti-gravity treadmill
items.description: A treadmill inside an air-pressurised chamber that lifts part of your body weight, used in rehab and for low-impact running.
items.adjustability: Air pressure sets how much body weight you carry.
items.buying_tips: Found in physio clinics and pro sports facilities; pay per session rather than buying.
items.safety: Follow your physio's progression plan for body-weight percentage.

items.name: Stationary bike
items.description: A seated exercise bike with a flywheel and adjustable resistance, for steady low-impact cardio.
items.adjustability: Seat height and fore-aft; handlebar on some.
items.buying_tips: Magnetic resistance is quieter and needs less upkeep than felt-pad friction.

items.name: Recumbent bike
items.description: A low exercise bike with a backrest and pedals out in front, easy on the back and hips and easy to get on and off.
items.buying_tips: Good for older users, back pain or rehab; check the seat slides far enough for your leg length.

items.name: Spin bike
items.description: A sturdy indoor cycle with a heavy flywheel, road-bike riding position and resistance knob, for class-style rides and intervals.
items.weight_options: Felt-pad friction or magnetic, flywheel 13–22 kg
items.adjustability: Seat and bar height and fore-aft; resistance knob.
items.buying_tips: Magnetic resistance, an emergency brake and clip-in pedals are worth paying for.
items.safety: Press the resistance knob down to brake; fixed-gear pedals keep spinning.

items.name: Smart bike
items.description: A connected indoor bike with automatic, app-controlled resistance, power measurement and often a screen for classes or virtual rides.
items.adjustability: Resistance set by app; fit adjusts to a road bike.
items.buying_tips: Check which apps it works with and whether a subscription is required to use the resistance features.

items.name: Bike trainer (turbo)
items.description: A stand that turns your own road or mountain bike into an indoor bike, either by clamping the rear wheel or replacing it (direct drive).
items.weight_options: Fluid, magnetic, fan or smart electromagnetic
items.adjustability: Smart units change resistance by app.
items.buying_tips: Direct-drive smart trainers are quieter and more accurate; check your bike's axle and cassette type.
items.safety: Put a mat underneath and a fan in front; you'll sweat a lot.
items.keywords: turbo trainer smart road bike zwift

items.name: Bike rollers
items.description: Three drums you ride your own bike on freely, without clamping it, which trains balance and smooth pedalling.
items.weight_options: Free rollers; some add magnetic resistance
items.buying_tips: Start next to a wall or in a doorway until you can balance.
items.safety: Ride beside something you can grab; falls are common at first.

items.name: Air / assault bike
items.description: A fan bike with moving arm handles: the harder you push and pull, the more resistance the fan gives. Brutal for intervals.
items.buying_tips: Belt-driven models (Echo, AssaultBike Elite) need less upkeep than chain drives.

items.name: Pedal exerciser
items.description: A small set of pedals with a resistance knob that you use under a desk or chair with your legs, or on a table with your arms.
items.buying_tips: Get one with a strap or rubber feet so it doesn't slide away from your chair.

items.name: Recumbent cross trainer
items.description: A seated full-body machine where you push foot pedals and move arm handles together, very low impact and used heavily in rehab.
items.adjustability: Seat swivels and slides; arm length adjusts.
items.buying_tips: Common in hospitals, senior centres and physio clinics; good for anyone who struggles to get on a bike.

items.name: Rowing machine
items.description: A sliding-seat erg where you drive with the legs and pull a handle, with fan air resistance. Full body, low impact.
items.buying_tips: The Concept2 RowErg is the gym standard; it holds its resale value and its numbers match everyone else's.

items.name: Water rower
items.description: A rowing machine whose resistance comes from paddles in a tank of water, giving a smooth, quiet, boat-like feel.
items.buying_tips: Looks good and stands upright for storage; numbers differ from a Concept2, so don't compare splits.

items.name: Magnetic rower
items.description: A quiet rowing machine using magnets for resistance at fixed levels, popular for flats and home use.
items.buying_tips: Cheap models have short rails; if you're over 185 cm check the inseam limit.

items.name: Hydraulic rower
items.description: A compact budget rower using one or two hydraulic pistons on swinging arms; cheap and small, but the stroke feels unlike real rowing.
items.buying_tips: Fine for a taste of rowing on a tight budget; pistons get hot and fade on long sessions.

items.name: Ski erg
items.description: A standing erg where you pull two handles down from overhead, like double-poling on cross-country skis, for upper-body-led cardio.
items.buying_tips: Needs about 2.3 m of ceiling; the wall-mount version saves floor space.

items.name: BikeErg
items.description: Concept2's fan-resistance indoor bike with the same monitor as their rower, used for comparable, measurable bike work.
items.adjustability: Seat and bar height; road-bike fit.
items.buying_tips: Accepts your own saddle and pedals; very low upkeep compared with friction spin bikes.

items.name: Upper body ergometer
items.description: A table-height hand-cranked bike for the arms, for cardio when the legs can't be used and for shoulder rehab or conditioning.
items.weight_options: Magnetic or air, light to heavy
items.adjustability: Crank height and seat adjust; can work forwards or backwards.
items.buying_tips: Common in physio clinics and adaptive gyms; a pedal exerciser on a table is the cheap home version.
items.keywords: arm bike ergometer ube hand crank

items.name: Swim ergometer
items.description: A bench you lie on face down and pull paddles or handles on cords, copying the swim stroke for dryland swim training.
items.buying_tips: Mainly for swimmers and triathletes; long stretch cords are the cheap alternative.

items.name: Stair climber
items.description: A machine with a revolving staircase you keep climbing, a very effective low-impact way to work the glutes and lungs.
items.buying_tips: Needs high ceilings and a lot of power; mostly a commercial-gym machine.
items.safety: Hold the rails lightly only; don't lean on them.

items.name: Step machine
items.description: A machine with two independent pedals you press down in turn, like climbing stairs without leaving the spot.
items.buying_tips: Look for independent pedals and a solid frame; cheap ones feel bouncy.

items.name: Mini stepper
items.description: A small floor stepper with two short pedals on hydraulic pistons, often with bands for the arms, that fits under a bed.
items.adjustability: Step height dial on some; twist versions.
items.buying_tips: Good for gentle activity in small spaces; not intense enough to replace a full stepper.

items.name: VersaClimber
items.description: A vertical climbing machine where arms and legs move together on handles and pedals, for very hard full-body, low-impact cardio.
items.weight_options: Hydraulic or air resistance; budget versions use body weight
items.buying_tips: Folding vertical climbers (MaxiClimber) cost far less but are much lighter-duty.

items.name: Jacob's ladder
items.description: An endless sloped ladder you climb on all fours; it moves at the speed you climb, for self-paced full-body cardio.
items.adjustability: Speed set by your climbing; hip belt.
items.buying_tips: Mostly seen in CrossFit and military-style gyms; needs a high ceiling.
items.safety: Wear the hip belt so you can't climb off the top.

items.name: Rope climber machine
items.description: An endless-rope machine you pull hand over hand against adjustable resistance, standing, seated or kneeling.
items.buying_tips: Great grip and back conditioning; a sled with a rope is the low-cost alternative.

items.name: Rotating climbing wall
items.description: A rolling climbing wall that turns as you climb so you stay near the floor, for endurance climbing and grip.
items.buying_tips: Rare and expensive; found in climbing gyms and some boutique studios.

items.name: Elliptical / cross trainer
items.description: A machine with foot pedals that move in an oval path and handles that swing with them, for low-impact full-body cardio.
items.weight_options: Magnetic, 8–25 levels; incline ramp on some
items.adjustability: Resistance, ramp, stride length on some.
items.buying_tips: A stride length of at least 50 cm feels natural for most adults.

items.name: Arc trainer
items.description: An elliptical-like machine with an arc-shaped foot path and high incline, putting more load on the glutes with less knee stress.
items.buying_tips: Mostly found in commercial gyms; try different incline settings to shift work to the glutes.

items.name: Lateral trainer
items.description: An elliptical that adds side-to-side motion to the stride, training the hips and inner and outer thighs.
items.buying_tips: Adds variety for skiers and court athletes; Precor's AMT has a variable stride rather than lateral motion.

items.name: Under-desk elliptical
items.description: A small pedal-only elliptical you use seated under a desk or chair, for gentle leg movement during the day.
items.buying_tips: Low and quiet; check your desk height leaves enough knee room.

items.name: Air walker
items.description: A simple frame with two swinging foot pedals that glide forward and back, a very gentle walking-style cardio machine.
items.buying_tips: Very cheap and folds flat, but intensity is limited; also common in outdoor fitness parks.

items.name: Cross-country ski machine
items.description: A machine with sliding foot skis and pull cords for the arms, copying classic cross-country skiing for full-body cardio.
items.weight_options: Friction flywheel and arm cord tension
items.adjustability: Leg and arm resistance separately; incline.
items.buying_tips: Mostly second-hand now; takes practice to coordinate arms and legs.

items.name: Slide board
items.description: A long slick board with stop bumpers at each end; you slide side to side in booties, like speed skating.
items.buying_tips: Longer boards are harder; booties must be kept clean to slide well.
items.safety: Wear the booties and keep shoes off the board.

items.name: Rebounder / mini trampoline
items.description: A small round trampoline for bouncing, jogging and light jumping, gentler on joints than jumping on the floor.
items.weight_options: Springs or bungee cords; 90–130 cm wide
items.buying_tips: Bungee-cord models are quieter and softer than steel springs; a handle bar helps balance.
items.safety: Keep it on a flat floor with clear space around it.

items.name: Jump rope
items.description: A skipping rope with handles for footwork, coordination and cheap, portable cardio.
items.weight_options: PVC, cable, beaded or weighted; length by height
items.buying_tips: Size it so the handles reach your armpits when you stand on the middle.

items.name: Speed rope
items.description: A thin coated-cable rope with bearing handles that spins very fast, used for double unders and fast footwork.
items.buying_tips: Bring spare cables; they fray on concrete.
items.safety: A thin cable stings when it hits; wear long socks at first.

items.name: Weighted jump rope
items.description: A thick or heavy rope, sometimes with weighted handles, that slows the rotation and works the shoulders and grip harder.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some have removable handle weights.
items.buying_tips: 0.5–1 lb ropes are good for learning; heavier ones are for short conditioning blocks.

items.name: Beaded jump rope
items.description: A rope made of plastic segments on a cord; its weight and feedback make it good for learning and for freestyle tricks.
items.buying_tips: Best rope for beginners and kids; durable outdoors.

items.name: Cordless jump rope
items.description: Two handles with short weighted tethers and no rope, for skipping motion where ceilings or space are too small.
items.buying_tips: Good for low ceilings and flats; doesn't train timing like a real rope.

items.name: Battle ropes
items.description: Heavy, thick ropes anchored at the middle that you whip in waves and slams for upper-body conditioning.
items.adjustability: Change length or thickness to adjust difficulty.
items.buying_tips: Poly-dacron ropes shed less than manila; 38 mm x 12 m suits most people.

items.name: Battle rope anchor
items.description: A wall or floor anchor, strap or weighted base that holds the middle of a battle rope in place.
items.weight_options: Wall bracket, floor plate or anchor strap
items.buying_tips: A strap around a rack post or heavy kettlebell works if you can't drill into a wall.

items.name: Push / pull sled
items.description: A weighted sled with push uprights you drive across turf, and a hook to drag with a harness or rope. Huge leg work without eccentric soreness.
items.weight_options: Sled 20–45 kg empty; load with plates
items.adjustability: High and low push handles on most.
items.buying_tips: Needs turf or a smooth outdoor surface; check runners suit your floor.

items.name: Drag sled
items.description: A simple flat metal sled with a plate post that you drag with a harness, straps or rope; cheaper and lighter than a push sled.
items.buying_tips: Works on grass or concrete; a car tyre with a rope is the DIY version.

items.name: Tank-style sled
items.description: A wheeled push sled with built-in adjustable brake resistance, so it works on any floor with no plates.
items.weight_options: Resistance levels 1–3+ by lever; some magnetic
items.adjustability: Brake lever sets resistance; push and pull.
items.buying_tips: Great for indoor gyms without turf; check the wheel type won't mark your floor.

items.name: Sled harness
items.description: A shoulder or waist harness with a strap or rope that hooks onto a sled, for forward and backward drags and sprints.
items.weight_options: Shoulder or waist belt; straps 2–4 m
items.buying_tips: Waist harnesses suit sprints; shoulder harnesses let you lean into heavy drags.

items.name: Speed parachute
items.description: A small parachute clipped to a waist belt that catches air as you sprint, adding resistance that grows with speed.
items.buying_tips: Needs a long open space and doesn't work well in strong wind.

items.name: Sprint resistance harness
items.description: A waist belt with a long elastic cord or strap held by a partner or anchor, for resisted sprints, release sprints and agility work.
items.buying_tips: A belt with a quick-release lets the partner let go for overspeed sprints.
items.safety: Check the cord for cracks before every session.

items.name: Plyo box
items.description: A sturdy box for box jumps, step-ups and depth drops. Wooden 3-in-1 boxes give three heights by flipping.
items.buying_tips: Check it's stable on every face; steel boxes are sturdier but hurt more on a miss.
items.safety: Step down rather than jumping down for reps.

items.name: Soft plyo box
items.description: A dense foam box, single or stackable, that forgives missed jumps and is safer for high reps and beginners.
items.buying_tips: Look for a heavy foam core and non-slip base; very light boxes slide.

items.name: Adjustable plyo box
items.description: A steel box or platform whose height adjusts with pins or stacked risers, so one box covers many jump heights.
items.buying_tips: Make sure the pins lock firmly and the top is non-slip.
items.safety: Re-check the pins before every jump session.

items.name: Agility ladder
items.description: A flat flexible ladder laid on the floor for fast footwork patterns, coordination and warm-ups.
items.buying_tips: Flat rungs are less likely to trip you; tape on the floor works if you have none.

items.name: Cones
items.description: Plastic cones or flat disc markers for laying out sprints, shuttle runs and change-of-direction drills.
items.weight_options: Disc 5 cm, cones 15–45 cm; sets of 10–50
items.buying_tips: Disc cones stack and travel easily; taller cones are easier to see in a big space.

items.name: Hurdles
items.description: Small plastic speed hurdles (15–30 cm) or adjustable hurdles for hops, bounds and stepping drills.
items.adjustability: Adjustable models set height by sliders.
items.buying_tips: Collapsible plastic hurdles are safest because they bend if you clip them.
items.safety: Use hurdles that fall over if you clip them.

items.name: Agility poles
items.description: Upright slalom poles on spiked or weighted bases for weaving, cutting and change-of-direction drills.
items.buying_tips: Spiked bases for grass; weighted bases for indoor or hard floors.

items.name: Reaction ball
items.description: A small rubber ball with knobbly sides that bounces unpredictably, for reaction time and hand-eye coordination.
items.buying_tips: Cheap and portable; tennis balls are an easier starting point.

items.name: Reaction lights
items.description: Wireless light pods that turn on in random or set orders; you sprint or reach to tap them off, for reaction and agility training.
items.buying_tips: Check the app's drill library and whether it needs a subscription.

items.name: Agility rings
items.description: Flat plastic rings that link into patterns on the floor for hopping and footwork drills.
items.buying_tips: More flexible layouts than a ladder; good for kids' sessions.

items.name: Medicine ball
items.description: A weighted ball for throws, passes, twists and loaded core work; rubber ones bounce back off walls and the floor.
items.weight_options: 1–12 kg (2–25 lb); rubber bouncing or soft
items.buying_tips: 3–5 kg suits most adults for throws; rubber bouncing balls are best for rebounds.
items.safety: Don't slam a bouncing ball; it can fly back at your face.

items.name: Slam ball
items.description: A heavy, dead-bounce ball with a thick shell, sand-filled so it doesn't bounce back when you slam it to the floor.
items.buying_tips: Textured shells are easier to grip with sweaty hands; heavy ones double as strongman-style shouldering balls.
items.safety: Slam on rubber flooring, not concrete or wood.

items.name: Wall ball
items.description: A large, soft-shelled medicine ball made to be thrown at a wall target and caught, as in CrossFit wall-ball shots.
items.buying_tips: Double-stitched synthetic leather lasts longest; 35 cm diameter is standard.

items.name: Wall-ball target
items.description: A wall-mounted target or rig attachment marking the standard height (3 m or 2.7 m) for wall-ball shots.
items.adjustability: Height fixed or adjustable on rig mounts.
items.buying_tips: A tape mark on a solid wall works fine at home.

items.name: Sandbell
items.description: A floppy, sand-filled disc bag with no handles that you slam, throw, carry and twist with.
items.buying_tips: Holds its shape poorly, which is the point; good for grip work.

items.name: Medicine ball rebounder
items.description: An angled trampoline net that throws a medicine ball straight back, so you can do throws and catches without a partner or wall.
items.buying_tips: Use a soft medicine ball; hard balls can damage the net.

items.name: Handled medicine ball
items.description: A medicine ball with one or two built-in handles, making it easier to hold for twists, chops, push-ups and kettlebell-style moves.
items.buying_tips: Handles make it unsuitable for slams or wall throws.

items.name: Rope medicine ball
items.description: A medicine ball on a rope or strap that you swing and slam into the ground or a wall for rotational power.
items.adjustability: Hold the rope shorter or longer.
items.buying_tips: Needs clear space; a sledgehammer and tyre is a similar alternative.
items.safety: Check nobody is within swinging range.
